items.prompt: What is wrong with Shirin's phone?
items.audio:
Shirin bought a new phone from an online shop three weeks ago. At first she loved it, but then the battery began to die very fast. She charged it in the morning, and by lunchtime it was empty. On Sunday she decided to call customer service.

She dialled the number on the shop's website and heard a recorded voice. It said, Press one for orders, press two for problems with a product, and press three to speak to a person. Shirin pressed two and waited for eight minutes while she listened to music. At last a man answered. His name was Kamran.

Kamran asked for her order number, which was in her email. Shirin read it slowly. He asked what the problem was, and she explained about the battery. He said she should turn the phone off and on, and then check the settings. Shirin tried it, but it did not help. Kamran said he was sorry and told her that the phone was still under guarantee for two years.

He offered two choices. She could send the phone back and wait ten days for a new one, or she could take it to a service centre in her city and get it repaired in three days. Shirin chose the second option because she needed a phone for work. Kamran sent her the address of the centre by text message.

He also gave her a case number, which was important. She wrote it on a piece of paper and thanked him. On Tuesday, the centre changed the battery for free. Shirin was very happy with the help and wrote a nice review online.

items.prompt: Where did Nodira see the sign?
items.audio:
Nodira is twenty years old, and she is looking for a part-time job. Last week she saw a sign in the window of a bookshop. It said, we need a helper, please call. She wrote the phone number in her notebook and called the shop the same afternoon.

The owner of the shop, Mr Hamidov, answered. Nodira said, Good afternoon, I am calling about the job in your window. Is it still free? He said yes and asked her to tell him about herself. Nodira said she was a student of English at the university, she studied in the morning, and she loved books. She also said she had worked in a cafe last summer and knew how to talk to customers.

Mr Hamidov explained the job. The helper would work from two in the afternoon until seven in the evening, four days a week. She would put books on the shelves, help customers find books, and use the computer at the cash desk. The pay was two dollars an hour, and she could take home one book every month.

Nodira asked if she could work on Saturdays, because she had lessons on Wednesday. Mr Hamidov said Saturdays were very busy, so he would be glad. He invited her to the shop for a short talk on Friday at four o'clock. She should bring her student card and a list of the books she liked best.

After the call, Nodira smiled all evening. She spent two hours making her list. She chose twelve books, and her favourite was a story about a young girl and a horse.

items.prompt: What time was the meeting?
items.audio:
Bekzod had an important meeting with his boss at nine o'clock on Monday. He woke up at seven, had breakfast, and left the house at eight. Everything was normal until he reached the bus stop. The bus did not come. He waited for twenty minutes, and the street was full of cars that did not move. There had been an accident near the bridge.

At eight forty, Bekzod understood that he would be late. He took his phone and called his boss, Mrs Saidova. She answered after four rings. Bekzod said, Good morning, Mrs Saidova. I am so sorry, but I will be late for our meeting. There is a big traffic jam near the bridge, and my bus is stuck.

Mrs Saidova was calm. She asked how late he thought he would be. Bekzod said maybe thirty minutes, but he was not sure. She said that was all right and told him they could start at nine thirty instead. She also asked him not to run, because the road was wet and dangerous.

Bekzod thanked her three times. Then he decided to get off the bus and walk to the metro station, which was only ten minutes away. He took the train, and it was fast. At nine twenty-five he arrived at the office, out of breath but happy.

In the meeting room, he said sorry again. Mrs Saidova smiled and said it was not his fault. After the meeting, Bekzod bought a small cake for the office as a way to say sorry. Everybody enjoyed it, and the boss said he was a very polite person.

At eight forty, Bekzod understood that he would be late. He took his phone and called his boss, Mrs Saidova. She answered after four rings. Bekzod said, Good morning, Mrs Saidova. I am so sorry, but I will be late for our meeting. There is a big traffic jam near the bridge, and my bus is stuck.

Bekzod thanked her three times. Then he decided to get off the bus and walk to the metro station, which was only ten minutes away. He took the train, and it was fast. At nine twenty-five he arrived at the office, out of breath but happy.

items.prompt: What did Laylo order?
items.audio:
Laylo ordered a pair of winter boots from a website. The boots were blue, size thirty-eight, and they cost forty dollars. The shop said the parcel would arrive in five days. On the fourth day, her phone rang while she was at the university.

A man said, Hello, this is the delivery company. My name is Rustam. I have a parcel for Laylo Nazarova. Are you at home? Laylo said she was not at home, because she was at university until four o'clock. Rustam said he was near her street at that moment and could wait only ten minutes. Laylo said that was too short.

They looked for a solution. Rustam suggested that he could leave the parcel with a neighbour. Laylo thought about it and said her neighbour, Mrs Tursunova, lived in the flat next to hers and was usually at home. She gave him the flat number, which was nine. Rustam said he would knock on the door, and if the neighbour was at home, he would leave the parcel with her.

Twenty minutes later, Rustam sent a text message. It said that Mrs Tursunova had taken the box, and he had taken a photo as proof. Laylo thanked him and wrote back that she would collect the parcel in the evening.

At five o'clock, she knocked at her neighbour's door. Mrs Tursunova gave her the box with a smile and offered her a cup of tea and some sweet cakes. Laylo opened the box at home. The boots were perfect, and they were warm and soft. She wore them the next morning.

items.prompt: Why is Mr Alimov leaving a message?
items.audio:
Hello Ravshan, this is Mr Alimov, your landlord. I am leaving you this message because I could not reach you on the phone. It is Tuesday morning, and I want to tell you some important things about the flat.

First, next Monday some workers will come to your building. They will change the old water pipes in all the flats. They will start at nine in the morning and finish at about three in the afternoon. During this time, there will be no water. Please fill some bottles on Sunday evening, so you can wash and drink. Also, one worker must enter the bathroom, so someone has to be at home. If you cannot be there, you can leave the key with Mrs Orlova on the second floor.

Second, I want to talk about the rent. It is due on the fifth of every month, and I have not received this month's payment yet. I am sure it is just a small mistake, but please send the money by Friday. You can send it to my bank account, as usual.

Third, you told me last week that the kitchen window does not close well. I looked for a carpenter, and he will visit you on Thursday afternoon at about five. Please show him the window, and he will repair it for free.

Finally, I hope you are happy in the flat. If you have any problems, please call me on my mobile phone after seven in the evening, because I work during the day. Thank you, and good luck with your studies. Goodbye for now.
options: He wants to sell the flat

items.audio:
On Saturday evening, Sevara wanted to watch a film with her sister, but the internet did not work. The little light on the router was red, and every page on her computer said no connection. She restarted the router three times, but nothing changed. Finally, she called her internet company.

A woman named Dilbar answered. She said, Good evening, thank you for calling. How can I help? Sevara explained the problem. Dilbar asked her to read the numbers on the back of the router. Then she asked if the other lights were green. Sevara said that only the power light was green, and the others were red. Dilbar said that this probably meant a problem on the line outside, not in the house.

She checked her computer and found that there was a damaged cable in Sevara's street. A repair team was already working on it. Dilbar said the internet would come back in about two hours, and she was very sorry for the trouble. She also promised that the company would take off one day from Sevara's monthly bill.

Sevara thanked her. Dilbar added that if the internet did not work by eleven at night, Sevara should call again, and the company would send a technician in the morning.

Since there was no film, the sisters decided to play a board game. They made popcorn and laughed for two hours. Just before ten, the router light turned green. Sevara said it was a nice evening anyway, and they did not need the internet to have fun.

items.prompt: What was Otabek doing when the phone rang?
items.audio:
On a quiet Sunday afternoon, Otabek was cleaning his room when his phone rang. The number began with a strange code, and he did not know it. He almost did not answer, but something made him press the green button. A voice said, Hello, Otabek, it is me, Daniel!

Otabek could not believe it. Daniel was his best friend from school, who moved to Canada six years ago. They had not spoken for a long time, because Daniel lost his old phone and Otabek did not have his new number. Now Daniel was calling from the city of Toronto.

Daniel said he found Otabek's number through a school friend on social media. He was so happy to hear his voice. They talked for almost an hour. Daniel told him about his life. He had a job in a bank, a small flat near a big lake, and a dog called Max. In winter, it was minus twenty degrees there, and he missed the warm weather of home.

Otabek told him about his own news. He had finished university, and he now worked as a teacher in a small school. Last year he got married, and his wife was expecting a baby in the spring. Daniel was very excited and said he would send a present.

Before they said goodbye, Daniel made a big announcement. He had bought a plane ticket, and he would visit Tashkent in July. Otabek promised to meet him at the airport. When the call ended, Otabek sat on the bed with a huge smile, and he could not stop thinking about July.

items.prompt: When is Aziz's first guitar lesson?
items.audio:
Aziz has his first guitar lesson on Tuesday afternoon at a small music school in Tashkent. His teacher is a friendly man called Mr. Brown, who has played the guitar for thirty years. The lesson starts at four o'clock and lasts forty-five minutes. Aziz arrives ten minutes early because he is a little nervous.

First, Mr. Brown shows Aziz how to hold the guitar. He says the back must touch the stomach and the left hand must stay relaxed. Aziz's guitar is old and brown, and it once belonged to his uncle Rustam. Mr. Brown checks the strings and says they are fine, but one string is a bit loose, so he tunes it carefully.

Next, they learn three easy chords. They are called G, C and D. Aziz's fingers hurt after only five minutes, and Mr. Brown laughs kindly. He says every beginner feels the same, and the pain goes away after two weeks. He also tells Aziz to practise every day, but only for fifteen minutes. Short practice is better than one long practice on Sunday.

At the end of the lesson, Aziz plays a very simple song called Happy Days. He makes four mistakes, but Mr. Brown says that is a good result for a first day. For homework, Aziz must learn the chord changes and play the song five times each evening. Mr. Brown also lends him a small notebook for writing down the chords.

Aziz pays twenty thousand som for the lesson. The next lesson is on Thursday at the same time. On the bus home, Aziz is tired but very happy. He is already thinking about the day when he can play a song for his mother at her birthday party in April.

The lesson starts at four o'clock and lasts forty-five minutes. Aziz arrives ten minutes early because he is a little nervous.

First, Mr. Brown shows Aziz how to hold the guitar. He says the back must touch the stomach and the left hand must stay relaxed. Aziz's guitar is old and brown, and it once belonged to his uncle Rustam. Mr. Brown checks the strings and says they are fine, but one string is a bit loose, so he tunes it carefully.

Next, they learn three easy chords. They are called G, C and D. Aziz's fingers hurt after only five minutes, and Mr. Brown laughs kindly. He says every beginner feels the same, and the pain goes away after two weeks. He also tells Aziz to practise every day, but only for fifteen minutes. Short practice is better than one long practice on Sunday.

At the end of the lesson, Aziz plays a very simple song called Happy Days. He makes four mistakes, but Mr. Brown says that is a good result for a first day. For homework, Aziz must learn the chord changes and play the song five times each evening. Mr. Brown also lends him a small notebook for writing down the chords.

Aziz pays twenty thousand som for the lesson. The next lesson is on Thursday at the same time. On the bus home, Aziz is tired but very happy. He is already thinking about the day when he can play a song for his mother at her birthday party in April.

items.prompt: What is Dilnoza's job at the club?
items.audio:
Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Samarkand Chess Club. My name is Dilnoza, and I am the president of the club. Tonight I want to tell you how we work and what you can expect in your first month.

The club meets every Monday and Friday at six o'clock in room twelve of the youth centre. Each meeting lasts two hours. On Mondays we practise with a coach named Mr. Karimov, who was a national champion in his youth. On Fridays we play friendly games and eat tea and biscuits, which our members bring from home. Please do not bring cola, because it is easy to spill on the boards.

We have thirty boards and about fifty members, so sometimes you must wait for a free place. Do not worry, because there is always something to do. You can watch a game, read a chess book from our small library, or solve a puzzle on the big wall board.

New members pay no money for the first month. After that, the price is ten thousand som every month, and students pay only half. The money is used to buy new chess clocks, because many of our old clocks are broken.

Every spring we have a big tournament. Last year, forty-two players took part, and a twelve-year-old girl called Madina won first prize. She beat three adults on the way to the final. The winner always gets a golden cup and a book about famous games.

If you are a complete beginner, ask for Mr. Karimov after the talk. He will give you a short test and then choose a group for you. Thank you for listening, and I hope you enjoy your time with us.

items.prompt: What time does the pool open from Monday to Saturday?
items.audio:
Welcome to the Sunrise Swimming Pool. This is the new schedule for the winter months, so please listen carefully.

The pool opens at seven o'clock in the morning and closes at nine o'clock in the evening from Monday to Saturday. On Sunday it opens later, at ten o'clock, and closes at six. We are closed on public holidays.

From seven to eight every morning, the pool is only for adults who want to swim lengths. The water is cooler at that time, and there are six quiet lanes. Between nine and eleven on Tuesday and Thursday, mothers and babies can use the small warm pool. The water there is thirty-two degrees, which is very comfortable for small children.

Children's lessons are on Wednesday and Saturday afternoons at four o'clock. Our teacher, Mr. Olimov, has two groups. Beginners learn to float and kick, and the advanced group learns the butterfly stroke. Each lesson lasts forty minutes, and a group has no more than eight children. A month of lessons costs eighty thousand som.

Please remember some important rules. Everyone must take a shower before entering the water. You must wear a swimming cap, and you cannot run on the wet floor. Small lockers are free, but you need to bring your own lock. If you forget it, you can buy one at the shop near the door for three thousand som.

This month we have a special offer. If you bring a friend on Friday evening, you both swim for half price. We also have a cafe next to the pool, where you can buy hot tea and fruit after your swim. We hope to see you soon at Sunrise.

items.prompt: Where does the photography walk take place?
items.audio:
On Saturday morning, Malika joins a photography walk in the old part of Bukhara. The group has eight people, and the guide is a young photographer called Jasur. They meet at half past seven in front of the big blue gate near the market.

Jasur explains that the best light is early in the morning, when the sun is low and the streets are still empty. He tells everyone to bring a small bag, a bottle of water and a hat, because the afternoon can be very hot. Malika has an old camera that her grandfather gave her. Jasur says that the camera does not matter. What matters is the way you look at things.

The group walks slowly for three hours. They take photos of the narrow streets, the blue domes and the old men who drink tea outside a small shop. Malika's favourite picture is a little boy who sells bread from a wooden cart. He smiles at her and holds up a round loaf. She asks his mother for permission before taking the picture, because Jasur says this is very polite.

At ten thirty, the group stops for breakfast in a family courtyard. They eat warm bread, honey and nuts, and they show each other their best photos on the small screens. Jasur gives each person one piece of advice. For Malika, he says, try to take pictures from a lower position, because it makes ordinary things look more interesting.

Before going home, Malika buys a postcard of the city for her sister. She is tired, but she feels proud. Next month, Jasur plans a night walk, and Malika is going to join it.

items.prompt: On which days does the team train?
items.audio:
Every Wednesday and Friday, the boys of the Lion Football Club train on a green field behind the school. Today it is Wednesday, and the coach, Mr. Bakhtiyor, is waiting for the players at five o'clock. There are fifteen boys in the team, and the youngest is ten years old.

The training begins with a slow run around the field. The boys run four times and then stretch their legs for five minutes. Mr. Bakhtiyor says that a good warm-up stops injuries. After that, the team practises passing in pairs. Sardor, the tallest boy, is a goalkeeper, so he works with the coach on catching high balls.

At half past five, the boys play a short game with two teams, red and yellow. Red wins by three goals to two. Timur scores two goals for the red team, and the coach praises him. But Timur is also late for the training, so he must carry the heavy bag of balls back to the school. The other boys laugh, and Timur smiles because he knows the rule.

At six o'clock, the coach gathers everyone in a circle. He reminds them about the match on Saturday against the Eagles, a team from the next town. The bus leaves at eight in the morning, and each player must bring a clean shirt, a bottle of water and an apple.

Before going home, the boys drink water and talk about their plans. Sardor says he wants to be a famous goalkeeper one day. Mr. Bakhtiyor tells him to practise hard, listen to advice and never give up. Then everyone shakes hands and says goodbye.

Every Wednesday and Friday, the boys of the Lion Football Club train on a green field behind the school. Today it is Wednesday, and the coach, Mr. Bakhtiyor, is waiting for the players at five o'clock. There are fifteen boys in the team, and the youngest is ten years old.

The training begins with a slow run around the field. The boys run four times and then stretch their legs for five minutes. Mr. Bakhtiyor says that a good warm-up stops injuries. After that, the team practises passing in pairs. Sardor, the tallest boy, is a goalkeeper, so he works with the coach on catching high balls.

At half past five, the boys play a short game with two teams, red and yellow. Red wins by three goals to two. Timur scores two goals for the red team, and the coach praises him. But Timur is also late for the training, so he must carry the heavy bag of balls back to the school. The other boys laugh, and Timur smiles because he knows the rule.

At six o'clock, the coach gathers everyone in a circle. He reminds them about the match on Saturday against the Eagles, a team from the next town. The bus leaves at eight in the morning, and each player must bring a clean shirt, a bottle of water and an apple.

Before going home, the boys drink water and talk about their plans. Sardor says he wants to be a famous goalkeeper one day. Mr. Bakhtiyor tells him to practise hard, listen to advice and never give up. Then everyone shakes hands and says goodbye.

items.prompt: Why could Nilufar not paint before?
items.audio:
Nilufar is fifty years old, and last month she started a painting class for adults at the town library. She always wanted to paint, but she was too busy with her job and her three children. Now the children are grown up, and she finally has time for herself.

The class is on Thursday evenings from six to eight. There are twelve students, and the teacher is an artist named Mrs. Ivanova. She is a patient woman with grey hair and a bright orange scarf. In the first lesson, she asks everyone to paint an apple, and she says that nobody must feel afraid of making mistakes.

Nilufar's apple looks more like a tomato, and the other students smile. But Mrs. Ivanova does not laugh. She shows Nilufar how to mix red and yellow to make a warmer colour, and how to leave a small white spot to show the light. After one hour, the apple looks much better.

In the second week, the class paints flowers. Mrs. Ivanova brings a big vase of sunflowers and puts it on a table in the middle of the room. Everyone sits around it, and the room becomes very quiet. Nilufar uses a lot of yellow and a little green, and she is happy with the result. She decides to hang the picture in her kitchen.

The course lasts eight weeks and costs one hundred and twenty thousand som. At the end, the library will hold a small exhibition, and every student can show one picture. Nilufar is already planning her work. She wants to paint her old garden in autumn, because it is her favourite place in the whole world.

items.prompt: When does the book club meet?
items.answer: the first Sunday of every month
items.audio:
The Friendly Pages Book Club meets on the first Sunday of every month in a quiet cafe near the park. There are nine members, and the oldest is a retired teacher named Mr. Yusupov. He is seventy-two years old, and he has read more than two thousand books in his life.

This month, the club discusses a short novel about a girl who lives on a farm in the mountains. Everyone read the book at home during the last four weeks. The meeting starts at three o'clock, and the first cup of tea is always free.

Gulnora, the youngest member, says that she loved the beginning of the story but found the ending too sad. Mr. Yusupov disagrees. He thinks that the ending is the best part, because it shows how brave the girl is. Then Bobur says that he did not enjoy the book at all. He prefers detective stories, and he thinks that nothing exciting happens on the farm. The members laugh, but they listen to him politely, because the club has a rule that every opinion is welcome.

After the discussion, the members choose the next book. They have three ideas, a funny story about a dog, a history book about the Silk Road and a love story from the nineteenth century. After a vote, the history book gets five votes, the dog story gets three, and the love story gets only one. So the club will read about the Silk Road.

Before leaving, each member takes a small paper with a question to think about at home. The next meeting is on the first Sunday of December. Everyone promises to read at least one chapter every week.
options: the first Sunday of every month
the last Friday of the month

items.prompt: What is the programme called?
items.audio:
Hello, gardeners, and welcome to our weekly radio programme, Green Hands. My name is Farida, and today I want to talk about growing tomatoes at home. Many people think it is difficult, but I promise you that it is easy if you follow a few simple steps.

First, choose the right time. In our region, the best time to plant small tomato plants outside is the middle of May, when the nights are no longer cold. If you plant them too early, the frost can kill them in one night. My neighbour, Mr. Hamidov, lost twelve plants last year for this reason.

Second, choose the right place. Tomatoes love the sun, so they need at least six hours of light every day. A wall that faces south is perfect. Dig a deep hole for each plant and put a little compost at the bottom. Leave about sixty centimetres between the plants, because they grow very big.

Third, water carefully. Many beginners give too much water, and the roots start to rot. It is better to water deeply two times a week than a little every day. Always water in the morning, and try to keep the leaves dry. Wet leaves can get a disease.

Here is my favourite tip. When the first small yellow flowers appear, put a thin stick next to each plant and tie the stem gently with a soft string. This helps the plant stand up straight, and the fruit does not touch the ground.

If you do all this, you can pick your first red tomatoes in July. Next week, I will talk about growing cucumbers. Goodbye, and happy gardening.

items.prompt: What time did they wake up?
items.audio:
Last Saturday, Eldor went fishing with his father and his cousin Anvar. They woke up at four o'clock in the morning, when the sky was still dark, and drove for an hour to a quiet lake in the hills. Eldor's mother gave them a basket with sandwiches, boiled eggs and a big bottle of tea.

The lake was very calm, and a white mist covered the water. His father said that fish are more active early in the morning, so they hurried to their place on a small wooden bridge. Eldor had a new fishing rod, which he got for his birthday in March. He was proud of it and held it carefully.

For the first two hours, nobody caught anything. Anvar became bored and started to talk loudly, and his uncle asked him to be quiet, because noise frightens the fish. Eldor laughed, but then he felt a strong pull on his line. He pulled up a silver fish that was about thirty centimetres long. His father said it was a carp, and everyone was very happy.

At noon, they sat under a big tree and ate their lunch. Anvar caught two small fish after lunch, but he put them back in the water, because they were too small. His father always teaches the boys to respect nature and to take only what they need.

In the afternoon, the weather changed, and it began to rain. The three of them ran to the car with their wet bags. They went home with one carp, which Eldor's mother cooked for dinner. Eldor says it was the tastiest fish of his life, and he wants to go again next month.

The lake was very calm, and a white mist covered the water. His father said that fish are more active early in the morning, so they hurried to their place on a small wooden bridge. Eldor had a new fishing rod, which he got for his birthday in March. He was proud of it and held it carefully.

For the first two hours, nobody caught anything. Anvar became bored and started to talk loudly, and his uncle asked him to be quiet, because noise frightens the fish. Eldor laughed, but then he felt a strong pull on his line. He pulled up a silver fish that was about thirty centimetres long. His father said it was a carp, and everyone was very happy.

At noon, they sat under a big tree and ate their lunch. Anvar caught two small fish after lunch, but he put them back in the water, because they were too small. His father always teaches the boys to respect nature and to take only what they need.

In the afternoon, the weather changed, and it began to rain. The three of them ran to the car with their wet bags. They went home with one carp, which Eldor's mother cooked for dinner. Eldor says it was the tastiest fish of his life, and he wants to go again next month.

items.prompt: When is the big show?
items.audio:
It is Thursday evening, and the school hall is full of music. The dance group Little Stars is preparing for a big show on the twentieth of May. There are fourteen girls and four boys in the group, and their teacher is a lively young woman named Shirin.

The rehearsal starts at five o'clock. First, everyone does warm-up exercises for ten minutes. Shirin says that dancers must have strong legs and a flexible back. Then the group practises a traditional dance with colourful dresses and fast music. The steps are not difficult, but the dancers must move at the same time, and this is the hard part.

Today, Shirin is not happy with the second half of the dance. Dilya, a shy girl with long black hair, keeps turning to the wrong side. The other dancers become confused, and the music has to stop three times. Shirin does not shout. She takes Dilya's hand and counts the steps slowly with her. After ten minutes, Dilya makes no more mistakes, and everybody claps.

At seven o'clock, the group takes a short break and drinks water. Shirin tells them about the costumes. Their mothers are sewing the dresses at home, and the boys will wear white shirts with red belts. The costumes will be ready by the end of April.

The rehearsal finishes at half past eight. Shirin reminds the dancers that there is one more rehearsal on Saturday morning, and this time they will practise on the real stage in the town theatre. The girls are excited and cannot stop talking all the way home.

items.prompt: When do the friends want to go hiking?
items.audio:
Sevara and her three friends are planning a hiking weekend in the Chimgan mountains. They want to go in the first weekend of June, because the weather is warm but not too hot. Sevara is the organiser, and she makes a careful plan in a notebook.

They will leave Tashkent on Saturday at six o'clock in the morning by minibus. The driver, Mr. Rahim, will take them to a small village at the foot of the mountain. The trip costs thirty thousand som for each person. From the village, they will walk for five hours along a path that goes through a green forest and then along a river.

The group will have lunch beside a waterfall at noon. Sevara is going to bring bread, cheese and cucumbers, and her friend Kamola will bring a big bag of apples. Each person must carry two litres of water, because there is no shop on the path.

At four o'clock, the friends will arrive at a camp at the top of a small hill. They have one big tent for four people. Sevara's brother lends them the tent and two warm sleeping bags, but the other two sleeping bags they must borrow from neighbours. In the evening, they will make a small fire, cook soup and look at the stars.

On Sunday, they will get up at seven o'clock and walk back down a different path, which is shorter. The minibus will wait for them in the village at one o'clock. Sevara reminds everyone to wear strong shoes, bring a jacket and take a small first aid kit. She is sure that it will be a great adventure.

items.prompt: What is the name of the show?
items.audio:
Welcome to Tasty Time, the cooking show for busy families. I am your host, Chef Munira, and today we are going to make a very popular dish called plov. It is easy, and you need only one big pot.

First, let us look at the ingredients. For six people, you need one kilogram of rice, one kilogram of beef, one kilogram of carrots, three onions and a little salt. You also need a glass of oil and one whole head of garlic. I always use yellow carrots, because they are sweeter than orange ones. Please wash the rice well and leave it in warm water for half an hour.

Now we heat the oil in the pot until it is hot. I put in the onions and fry them until they become golden brown. Then I add the meat, cut into medium pieces, and cook it for fifteen minutes. The smell is wonderful already. Next, I add the carrots, which I cut into long thin strips, and I cook everything for another ten minutes.

Here comes the secret. I pour in two glasses of hot water and add a spoon of cumin. I let it simmer on low heat for forty minutes. This part is called the zirvak, and it gives the dish its rich flavour. After that, I put the rice on top, but I never stir it. I add more water, so that it covers the rice by about two centimetres.

When the water disappears, I make small holes with a spoon, put the garlic in the middle and cover the pot. After twenty minutes, the plov is ready. Serve it hot with a fresh salad of tomatoes and onions. Next week, we will make samsa. Until then, enjoy your meal.

The city cycling club has a new Sunday route, and the leader, Mr. Tursunov, is telling the members about it. The route is called the Green Ring, and it is thirty-six kilometres long. It starts and finishes at the main bus station, and most people need about three hours to cycle it.

The group will meet at eight o'clock in front of the station. Mr. Tursunov asks everyone to arrive ten minutes early, so that he can check the bicycles. Every cyclist must wear a helmet. Anyone without one cannot join the ride.

The first part of the route goes along a flat road beside the river. It is very quiet, and there are many tall trees. After ten kilometres, the group reaches a small bridge, where they stop for five minutes to drink water. Then the road goes up a long hill. This is the hardest part, and it is about four kilometres long. Mr. Tursunov says that beginners should go slowly and use a low gear. Nobody is in a hurry.

At the top of the hill, there is a lovely park with a lake. The club will stop here for a picnic lunch at eleven o'clock. Please bring your own food, because there is no cafe. After the rest, the road goes down, and the last twelve kilometres are easy and fast.

The ride is free for club members. Other people pay five thousand som, and the money is used for repairing old bicycles for children. If it rains, the ride moves to the next Sunday. Mr. Tursunov hopes that at least twenty people will come, and he promises that everybody will have a wonderful day.

items.prompt: Who organised the Volunteer Day?
items.audio:
On the last Saturday of September, the students of School Number Twelve took part in a Volunteer Day in their neighbourhood. The organiser was the English teacher, Mrs. Karimova, and she asked every class to choose one useful job.

The seventh grade decided to clean the small park next to the school. Twenty students came at nine o'clock with gloves, plastic bags and brooms. They picked up bottles and paper from the grass, and in two hours they filled thirty bags. A boy named Jamshid also found a broken bench, and his father, a carpenter, repaired it with new wood.

The eighth grade went to a home for old people on Navoi Street. They did not clean or paint. Instead, they talked to the old people, played chess with them and read poems aloud. A lady named Mrs. Zebo, who is eighty-five, told the girls stories about her childhood. She said that it was the nicest morning she had had for a year.

The ninth grade planted trees along the school fence. The city gave them forty small trees for free. Each student planted at least two, and they watered every one carefully. They wrote their names on little wooden signs, so that people can see who planted each tree.

At one o'clock, everyone met in the school yard for a free lunch. The parents cooked soup and bread for all the volunteers. Mrs. Karimova thanked the students and said she was very proud of them. She also announced that the school will organise a second Volunteer Day in spring, and many students raised their hands to join again.

items.prompt: How old is the grandfather now?
items.audio:
My grandfather Rustam is seventy-eight years old, and last Sunday he told us about his youth. He was born in a small village near Samarkand. When he was a boy, there was no electricity in the village, so the family used oil lamps in the evening. He walked five kilometres to school every day, and in winter his feet were often cold because his shoes had holes in them.

His father was a farmer who grew cotton and melons. Every summer, my grandfather helped him in the fields from five in the morning until noon. He says it was hard work, but he was never unhappy. After work, he and his friends swam in a small river and played football with a ball made of old rags.

When he was sixteen, he left the village and went to Tashkent to study at a technical school. He lived in a tiny room with three other boys. They had one table, one lamp and very little money, so they ate bread and tea for breakfast almost every day. At the weekends, they walked around the city and looked at the tall buildings, because they had never seen anything like them before.

In Tashkent he met my grandmother, Dilfuza, at a bus stop. It was raining, and she did not have an umbrella. He gave her his, and she laughed and said she would bring it back tomorrow. She did, and one year later they got married.

At the end of his story, my little brother asked if life was better in those days. Grandfather smiled and said it was different. They had less, but they helped each other more. Now we have phones and computers, and that is good too. But he asked us to visit him often.

items.prompt: Where does Malika work now?
items.audio:
My friend Malika has a new job, and yesterday she called me to talk about her first week. She now works as a receptionist at a hotel in Bukhara. Before that, she worked in a clothes shop for two years, but she did not enjoy it because the shop was small and the hours were long.

The hotel is a beautiful old house with a green garden in the middle. On Monday, her manager, Mr Karimov, showed her around the building. There are twenty rooms, a small restaurant and a roof terrace where guests drink tea in the evening. Malika says the terrace is her favourite place, because you can see the old blue domes of the city.

Her work starts at eight in the morning and finishes at four in the afternoon. She answers the phone, writes down bookings and helps guests with their questions. Many guests come from other countries, so she speaks English every day. At first she was nervous, and on Tuesday she forgot the name of a German guest. Luckily the man laughed and told her not to worry.

The money is better than in the shop, and she also gets a free lunch. The only problem is the travel. She lives twelve kilometres from the hotel and goes by bus, which takes forty minutes. Her brother says he can lend her his old bicycle, but she thinks the road is too busy.

Malika told me that she wants to learn Spanish next year, because many tourists come from Spain. I told her that I am proud of her. On Saturday we are going to meet in a cafe, and she will bring photos of the hotel.

items.prompt: When did the wedding take place?
items.audio:
Last month my sister Nigora got married, and I want to tell you about the day. The wedding was in the middle of May, on a warm and sunny Saturday. About two hundred people came, and our house was full of flowers from early in the morning.

The day began at six, when my aunts came to help my sister get ready. My mother cooked all night with two neighbours, and by seven in the morning there were big plates of plov, salads and sweet cakes on the tables in the garden. I was in charge of the music, so I tested the speakers three times. One of them did not work, and I had to borrow another one from my cousin.

The ceremony was at noon. My sister wore a long white dress and a gold necklace that belonged to our grandmother. Her husband, Jasur, wore a dark blue suit and looked very nervous. When he saw her, he forgot the words he had learned, and everybody laughed. Then my father gave a short speech. He said that he was proud of both of them, and he started to cry a little.

After lunch, we danced for four hours. Even my grandfather danced, which surprised everyone. In the evening, the young couple cut a big cake with strawberries on top. Then they left in a white car decorated with ribbons.

They are now on holiday by the sea in Turkey for ten days. Yesterday my sister sent me a message with a photo of the beach. I miss her already, but I am very happy for her.

items.prompt: Where did the narrator find the photo?
items.audio:
Last weekend I was cleaning my grandmother's wardrobe when I found an old black and white photo. In the picture there were six people standing in front of a small house. I took it to the kitchen and asked her who they were.

Grandmother put on her glasses and smiled. She said the photo was from nineteen seventy-four, the summer she was fifteen. The tall man in the middle was her father, my great-grandfather Hamid. He was a train driver, and he always wore a grey hat, even at home. Next to him stood her mother, who is holding a baby. The baby was her little brother Olim, who is now a doctor in Fergana.

Then she pointed to a girl with long dark hair. That was Grandmother herself. She said she hated the dress she was wearing, because it was too big and had belonged to her older cousin. The photographer was a neighbour who had just bought a camera, and he made everyone stand still for a whole minute. A small boy at the end of the line moved his head, and that is why his face looks strange in the picture.

The last person in the photo was a dog called Tulpor. Grandmother said he followed the children everywhere and once ate a whole loaf of bread from the table. They all loved him, and he lived for thirteen years.

I asked if I could have a copy. She said I could keep the photo, but only if I wrote the names of everyone on the back. So I did it carefully with a blue pen, and now the photo is in a frame on my desk.

items.prompt: How old was the narrator when she saw snow?
items.audio:
One of my happiest childhood memories is the day I saw snow for the first time. I was six years old, and we lived in a small flat in Termez, where winters are usually mild. That year, in January, my uncle invited us to his house in the mountains near Tashkent.

We travelled by train for a whole day. I sat by the window with my little sister Zebo, and we counted the cows we saw. When we arrived, it was already dark, and my uncle's wife gave us hot soup and warm blankets. I was so tired that I fell asleep immediately.

In the morning, I looked out of the window, and the whole world was white. I did not believe my eyes. I ran outside in my pyjamas, and my mother shouted at me to put on my boots. The snow was soft and cold, and it was higher than my knees. I tried to eat some, because I thought it was like ice cream. It tasted of nothing, and my cousins laughed at me.

After breakfast, we built a snowman in the yard. We used a carrot for the nose and two black stones for the eyes. My uncle gave us his old red scarf and a funny hat. Then we went down a hill on a plastic bag, and I fell off three times. My hands were red, and my nose was running, but I did not want to go home.

We stayed there for one week. When we left, I cried on the train, because I wanted to take the snowman with me. My mother said that I could keep the memory forever, and she was right.

items.prompt: What does Sardor study in Canada?
items.audio:
My cousin Sardor lives in Canada, and we talk on the phone every second Sunday. He moved there three years ago to study computer science. Last night he called me, and I want to share his news with you.

Sardor lives in a city called Toronto, which is very big and very cold in winter. Last January the temperature fell to minus twenty-five degrees. He says that on some mornings his bus did not come, and he had to walk to the university in deep snow. He bought a thick coat and special boots, but he still felt cold all the time.

He shares a flat with two students, one from India and one from Brazil. They take turns to cook, and every Friday they have an international dinner. Sardor cooked plov last week, and his friends liked it so much that they asked for more. The Brazilian boy said it was the best rice he had ever tasted. My cousin was very proud.

He also has a part-time job in a library, three evenings a week. He earns enough money to pay for his food and books. His English is now very good, but at first it was difficult. In the first month, he ordered a sandwich in a cafe and got a bowl of soup, because he did not understand the waiter.

Sardor misses his family and Uzbek bread most of all. He says he will come home next summer for a month. My mother is already planning a big dinner, and I cannot wait to see him again.

items.prompt: How long did Mrs Saidova teach at the school?
items.audio:
Today I want to tell you about Mrs Gulnora Saidova, who taught English at our school for thirty-five years. She retired last week, and on Friday we had a small party for her in the school hall.

Mrs Saidova started her career in nineteen eighty-nine in a village school with only forty students. There was no heating in the classrooms, so the children wore their coats during lessons. She had one old book and a small blackboard, but she made her lessons fun with songs and games. Many of those students still remember the songs today.

Ten years later, she moved to our city and began to teach at our school. She says the biggest change in her career was the arrival of computers. At first she was afraid of them and asked a young teacher to help her. After a few months, she was making slideshows and showing English films in class. She often said that a good teacher never stops learning.

During the party, five former students gave speeches. One of them, a doctor named Anvar, said that Mrs Saidova believed in him when he failed an exam. She gave him extra lessons every Tuesday and Thursday after school, and he passed the next time. He gave her a big bunch of white roses.

When it was her turn to speak, she was crying a little. She thanked everyone and said that the best part of her job was watching students grow up. She is not going to stay at home, though. Next month she will start a free English club for children in the library, and I plan to be the first to join.

items.prompt: Where was Bell born?
items.audio:
Today I would like to talk about Alexander Graham Bell, the man who invented the telephone. He was born in Edinburgh, in Scotland, in eighteen forty-seven. His father and grandfather both taught people how to speak clearly, and his mother was almost deaf. Because of this, Alexander became interested in sound from a very young age.

As a boy, he was curious about everything. When he was twelve, he made a machine to clean wheat for a friend's father. It was simple, but it worked well. He also loved music and played the piano beautifully. At the age of twenty-three, he moved with his family to Canada, and a year later he started to work in the United States as a teacher of deaf children.

In his free time, he worked on ideas for sending the human voice through a wire. He worked with a young helper called Thomas Watson, usually at night in a small room. They tried many times, and many times they failed. Then, in March eighteen seventy-six, Bell spilled some acid on his clothes and shouted to Watson in the next room. Watson heard his voice through the machine and ran in. These were the first words ever sent by telephone.

The telephone made Bell famous, and he became rich. But he never stopped inventing. He worked on flying machines, boats and a metal detector. He also helped deaf people all his life, and he said he was happiest when working with children.

Bell died in nineteen twenty-two. On the day of his funeral, all the telephones in North America were silent for one minute, to show respect for him.

items.prompt: Who taught the grandmother to make manti?
items.audio:
In my family, there is one recipe that everybody loves: my grandmother's manti. She learned to make them from her own mother, and now she is teaching me. Last Saturday I spent the whole afternoon in her kitchen, and I want to tell you how it went.

First, we made the dough. Grandmother mixed flour, water, a little salt and one egg. She said the dough must rest for thirty minutes, so we drank tea while we waited. Then we cut the meat. She never uses a machine, because she says that cutting the meat with a knife gives a better taste. We mixed it with onions, black pepper and a bit of pumpkin, which makes the manti soft and sweet inside.

The hard part was the shape. Grandmother rolled the dough very thin, cut it into squares and put a spoon of meat in the middle of each one. Then she folded the corners together like a little hat. Mine looked terrible. Some were too big, and others opened in the water. She laughed and said her first ones looked even worse.

We steamed the manti for forty minutes in a special pot with three levels. The smell filled the house, and my brothers came to the kitchen to ask when dinner would be ready. We ate them with yoghurt and a little hot sauce.

At the end of the day, my grandmother gave me an old notebook. It had the recipe written in her mother's handwriting. She told me to keep it for my own children one day, and I promised her that I would.

In my family, there is one recipe that everybody loves: my grandmother's manti. She learned to make them from her own mother, and now she is teaching me. Last Saturday I spent the whole afternoon in her kitchen, and I want to tell you how it went.

First, we made the dough. Grandmother mixed flour, water, a little salt and one egg. She said the dough must rest for thirty minutes, so we drank tea while we waited. Then we cut the meat. She never uses a machine, because she says that cutting the meat with a knife gives a better taste. We mixed it with onions, black pepper and a bit of pumpkin, which makes the manti soft and sweet inside.

The hard part was the shape. Grandmother rolled the dough very thin, cut it into squares and put a spoon of meat in the middle of each one. Then she folded the corners together like a little hat. Mine looked terrible. Some were too big, and others opened in the water. She laughed and said her first ones looked even worse.

We steamed the manti for forty minutes in a special pot with three levels. The smell filled the house, and my brothers came to the kitchen to ask when dinner would be ready. We ate them with yoghurt and a little hot sauce.

At the end of the day, my grandmother gave me an old notebook. It had the recipe written in her mother's handwriting. She told me to keep it for my own children one day, and I promised her that I would.

items.prompt: How many years passed since they finished school?
items.audio:
Last Saturday I went to a reunion with my old classmates. It was twenty years since we finished school, and Aziza, our former class leader, organised everything. We met at six in the evening in a restaurant near our old school.

I was nervous before I went. I thought nobody would remember me, because I was a quiet boy who sat at the back of the room. But when I walked in, a tall man shouted my name and gave me a big hug. It was Farhod, my best friend, whom I had not seen for twelve years. He is now a pilot and lives in Dubai. He looked so different with his beard that I did not recognise him at first.

About twenty-five people came. Some of them had changed a lot. Our funniest classmate, Dilnoza, is now a serious judge. Our worst student, Eldor, owns a successful furniture company and drove up in a new car. Everyone laughed when he said that his maths teacher would never believe it.

Aziza had brought a box of old photos, and we looked at them for an hour. There was one of our class trip to the lake in the ninth grade, when the bus broke down and we had to walk for three hours. We remembered how tired we were, but also how much fun it was.

At ten o'clock, our old teacher, Mr Yusupov, arrived and gave a short speech. He said he was proud of all of us. We promised to meet again in five years. I went home late, but I felt very happy.

items.prompt: Why did the narrator wake up at five?
items.answer: He was too excited to sleep
items.audio:
My first day at university was last September, and I will never forget it. I woke up at five in the morning because I was too excited to sleep. My mother made me a big breakfast of eggs and bread, and my father drove me to the station. He gave me a small bag with sandwiches and told me to be brave.

The university is in the centre of the city, and it took me one hour to get there by train. When I arrived, I could not believe how big the buildings were. There were hundreds of students in the yard, and everybody seemed to know where to go. I felt small and lost. I took out my paper with the room number, which was three hundred and twelve, but I could not find it.

A girl with red glasses saw my face and asked if I needed help. Her name was Kamola, and she was also in the first year. She was studying the same subject as me, which was economics. We walked up the stairs together, and finally found the room on the third floor. We were ten minutes late, and the teacher gave us a strange look, but he said nothing.

The lesson was about money and banks. I understood only half of it, but Kamola shared her notes with me afterwards. At lunchtime, we met two boys from our group, Otabek and Ravshan, and we ate together in a noisy canteen. By the afternoon, I was not afraid any more.

When I came home in the evening, I was very tired but happy. I told my family everything, and my little sister asked me to take her there one day.

items.prompt: How old was the narrator on his first day?
items.audio:
Let me tell you about the most embarrassing mistake of my life. It happened two years ago, when I was a young teacher on my first day in a new school. I was twenty-three, and I wanted everyone to think that I was serious and clever.

The school was far from my home, so I got up very early and took two buses. I arrived at seven thirty, which was one hour before the first lesson. The building was empty and quiet. I walked along the corridor and found a room with a sign on the door that said Teachers. I went in, sat down in a big chair and started to read my notes.

After a few minutes, a tall man with grey hair came in. He looked at me with surprise and said hello. I stood up and introduced myself as the new English teacher. He smiled and said he was pleased to meet me. We talked for ten minutes about the school and the students. I thought that he was a friendly colleague, and I even asked him where I could buy a coffee.

Then the bell rang, and the room filled with teachers. One of them whispered to me that the man was Mr Alimov, the director of the school. I was so shocked that I dropped my notes on the floor. Worse still, the chair I was sitting in was his own, and nobody had told me.

Luckily, the director was very kind. He laughed and said that he had never met a teacher who gave him orders on the first day. Now we often joke about it, and every morning he brings me a cup of coffee.

The school was far from my home, so I got up very early and took two buses. I arrived at seven thirty, which was one hour before the first lesson. The building was empty and quiet. I walked along the corridor and found a room with a sign on the door that said Teachers. I went in, sat down in a big chair and started to read my notes.

After a few minutes, a tall man with grey hair came in. He looked at me with surprise and said hello. I stood up and introduced myself as the new English teacher. He smiled and said he was pleased to meet me. We talked for ten minutes about the school and the students. I thought that he was a friendly colleague, and I even asked him where I could buy a coffee.

Then the bell rang, and the room filled with teachers. One of them whispered to me that the man was Mr Alimov, the director of the school. I was so shocked that I dropped my notes on the floor. Worse still, the chair I was sitting in was his own, and nobody had told me.

Luckily, the director was very kind. He laughed and said that he had never met a teacher who gave him orders on the first day. Now we often joke about it, and every morning he brings me a cup of coffee.

items.prompt: How old is Timur?
items.audio:
Last month, a boy named Timur saved a little girl from a river, and the whole town is talking about it. Timur is only fourteen years old, and he lives in a village near the Chirchiq river.

It happened on a hot Sunday afternoon in July. Timur was fishing on the bank with his uncle when they heard a scream. A girl of six, whose name was Madina, was playing near the water and fell in. The river was fast and deep because of the rain in the previous week. Her older brother stood on the bank and shouted for help, but he could not swim.

Without thinking, Timur took off his shoes and jumped into the water. He is a strong swimmer, because he goes to a swimming club twice a week. He reached the girl in about thirty seconds and held her head above the water. The river was carrying them away, so his uncle ran along the bank and threw a long rope. Timur caught it with one hand, and the two men pulled them both to safety.

Madina was frightened and coughing, but she was not hurt. An ambulance took her to the hospital, and she went home the same evening. Her parents cried with happiness and thanked Timur many times.

Last Friday, the mayor of the town gave Timur a medal and a certificate in a special ceremony. When a journalist asked him how he felt, Timur said he was not a hero. He said that anyone would do the same. But I think that his courage was very special, and I hope that I can be as brave as he is.

items.prompt: Why did the narrator want a job?
items.audio:
Last summer I worked for the first time, and I learned a lot about life. I am seventeen, and I wanted to earn money for a new laptop. My cousin knew the owner of an ice cream shop in the park, and he found me a job there for two months.

My day began at nine in the morning. First I cleaned the tables and the floor, then I prepared the fruit for the day. The shop had twelve different flavours, and my favourite was the pistachio. My boss, a kind woman called Mrs Rahimova, taught me how to make a perfect ball of ice cream. At first mine were too small, and customers looked at me with disappointment.

The hardest part was the heat. In July the temperature was forty degrees, and the line of customers was sometimes thirty people long. I often stood for six hours without sitting down. But I also met many interesting people. One old man came every day at noon and ordered the same thing, a cup of vanilla with two cherries. After a week, I started to prepare it before he asked.

I made one big mistake in August. I dropped a whole box of cold strawberry ice cream on the floor. It made a huge pink mess, and I wanted to disappear. Mrs Rahimova only smiled and said that every cook makes a mess sometimes. She helped me to clean it.

At the end of the summer, I had enough money for the laptop and a little more. Mrs Rahimova gave me a small present, a pair of red gloves, and said that I could come back next year. I will gladly accept her offer.

My day began at nine in the morning. First I cleaned the tables and the floor, then I prepared the fruit for the day. The shop had twelve different flavours, and my favourite was the pistachio. My boss, a kind woman called Mrs Rahimova, taught me how to make a perfect ball of ice cream. At first mine were too small, and customers looked at me with disappointment.

The hardest part was the heat. In July the temperature was forty degrees, and the line of customers was sometimes thirty people long. I often stood for six hours without sitting down. But I also met many interesting people. One old man came every day at noon and ordered the same thing, a cup of vanilla with two cherries. After a week, I started to prepare it before he asked.

I made one big mistake in August. I dropped a whole box of cold strawberry ice cream on the floor. It made a huge pink mess, and I wanted to disappear. Mrs Rahimova only smiled and said that every cook makes a mess sometimes. She helped me to clean it.

At the end of the summer, I had enough money for the laptop and a little more. Mrs Rahimova gave me a small present, a pair of red gloves, and said that I could come back next year. I will gladly accept her offer.

items.prompt: When did Florence Nightingale live?
items.answer: From eighteen twenty to nineteen ten
items.audio:
Good morning, everyone. Today I would like to talk about my hero, Florence Nightingale. She was a British nurse who lived from eighteen twenty to nineteen ten, and she changed the way hospitals work all over the world.

Florence was born in a rich family in Italy, in a city called Florence, and that is where her name comes from. Her parents wanted her to marry a rich man and live a quiet life. But when she was seventeen, she felt that she must help sick people. Her family was not happy about this, because nursing was not a respected job at that time. She did not listen to them and studied hard.

In eighteen fifty-four, a terrible war began in Crimea, and many soldiers were hurt. Florence went there with thirty-eight other nurses. The hospital was dirty, cold and full of rats. Many soldiers died, not from wounds, but from disease. Florence worked day and night to clean the rooms, bring fresh air and give the men good food. In a few months, the number of deaths fell a lot. At night, she walked through the wards with a small lamp to check on every patient. The soldiers called her the Lady with the Lamp, and they loved her.

After the war, she opened a school for nurses in London. She also wrote books and used numbers and charts to show doctors how to save lives. She was the first woman to join the Royal Statistical Society.

I admire her because she was brave and never gave up, even when people laughed at her. She teaches us that one person can make the world better. Thank you for listening.
options: From eighteen twenty to nineteen ten
From nineteen twenty to two thousand
From seventeen twenty to eighteen ten
